_nota: Inglés del Paso 3 · El tipo de estabilidad. Calco parcial. OJO con «esencial»: las listas sin id se emparejan por POSICIÓN, así que el bloque 9 (tiraTornillos) va como objeto vacío para no descolocar los demás.
subtitulo: There are only two kinds of stability; in one fracture they can coexist by zone
preguntaClave: What kind of stability does this fracture need in order to heal and in order to work?
sintesis: There are only two kinds of stability. Perren's strain theory tells you which one applies: a reconstructable line and an articular surface → absolute, and direct healing; a comminuted component → relative, and healing by callus. When both coexist in the same fracture, one is assigned to each zone and the two principles are combined in a single construct. What is comminuted is never compressed.
objetivos: Understand stability as a means to a biology, not as an end in itself
Apply Perren's strain theory to decide between absolute and relative
Accept that a comminuted component does NOT allow absolute stability
Assign a stability to each zone and combine both principles in a single construct
Dose relative stability with the working length and the stiffness of the construct

decisiones.pregunta: How many mechanical zones does this fracture have?
decisiones.ayuda: A fracture can have a single component, or two with different demands: an articular block that has to be rebuilt, and a metaphyseal or diaphyseal component separating it from the shaft. Each zone is assigned its own stability.

criterios: The whole fracture answers to the same mechanical demand
Purely diaphyseal, or articular with no metaphyseal component to solve

opciones.etiqueta: Two zones: articular block and metaphyseal component
criterios: An articular surface that has to be rebuilt
A metaphyseal or diaphyseal component separating it from the shaft
The pattern of complex tibial plateau, pilon and distal humerus

decisiones.ayuda: There are only two. Absolute is the absence of interfragmentary motion under functional load; relative is controlled micromotion, proportional to the load.

criterios: Compression that generates friction and closes the gap
Demands a reconstructable line and an anatomical reduction
Strain below 2%, which is what lamellar bone tolerates
Controlled micromotion that stimulates callus
It is enough to restore alignment, length and rotation
Callus tolerates 10 to 15% strain

decisiones.ayuda: The articular surface does not tolerate micromotion: step-off and motion generate post-traumatic arthritis.

criterios: Anatomical reduction and interfragmentary compression
This is what an articular surface almost always demands
Exceptional: only if the articular block cannot be rebuilt
Check first whether the real indication is an arthroplasty

decisiones.pregunta: Metaphyseal or diaphyseal component: which stability?
decisiones.ayuda: If that component is complex, multifragmentary or comminuted, it does NOT allow absolute stability: there is nothing to compress without devitalising it.

criterios: Bridging of the comminuted component
Comminution spreads the strain and favours callus
It respects the blood supply of the intermediate fragments
Only if that component is a SIMPLE, reconstructable line
If it is comminuted, this option is a mechanical error

decisiones.pregunta: How are you going to dose the relative stability?
decisiones.ayuda: It is not «less fixation»: it is a calculated amount of motion. These are the real levers of the construct, and almost all of them are decided at the table, not in the catalogue.

criterios: It is the distance between the innermost screws on either side of the fracture: the length of plate that actually works
It is the dominant lever: it governs axial and torsional stiffness above any other factor
Omitting the screw next to the fracture on each side leaves the construct almost TWICE as flexible, in compression and in torsion
In practice: leave two or three holes empty on each side of the fracture

opciones.etiqueta: Plate · Raise the plate span ratio
criterios: Length of the plate divided by the length of the fracture
Above 2 or 3 in comminuted fractures; above 8 or 10 if the line is simple
A long plate spreads the load and lowers what each screw carries

opciones.etiqueta: Plate · Lower the plate screw density
criterios: Screws inserted divided by holes in the plate
Below 0.5 in comminuted fractures; below 0.3 or 0.4 if the line is simple
Filling every hole gives no more stability: it gives more stiffness, less callus and no margin

opciones.etiqueta: Plate · Three screws per fragment, well spread
criterios: Beyond three per fragment axial stiffness no longer rises; beyond four neither does torsional
Spread them along the fragment instead of grouping them near the fracture
The fourth and fifth screws buy no stability: they spend bone and holes
An internal fixator: it does not press the plate against the bone and preserves the periosteal blood supply
Holds osteoporotic bone and a comminuted metaphysis
But it suppresses motion at the near cortex: without enough working length it is too stiff

opciones.etiqueta: Plate · Lift it 2 to 5 mm off the bone
criterios: Only with a locked plate, which does not need to rest on the bone to stabilise
It reduces the stiffness of the construct and respects the periosteum
Going further lengthens the lever arm on the screws and brings forward implant failure

opciones.etiqueta: Plate · Dynamic locking or far cortical locking screws
criterios: They grip only the far cortex; the shaft flexes inside the medullary canal
They give motion back to the near cortex and with it a symmetrical callus
It is the direct answer to the asymmetrical callus of the conventional locked plate
A lower elastic modulus: the construct works somewhat more elastically
It is fine tuning; it is no substitute for the working length

opciones.etiqueta: Nail · Working length of the nail
criterios: With cortical contact, it is the distance between the zones where the nail rests on the endosteum
Without cortical contact, it is the whole distance between the innermost locking bolts
That is why a comminuted fracture treated with a nail is always far less stiff than it looks
Bending stiffness rises with the fourth power of the radius
It raises stiffness A LOT: it is the lever for asking for LESS motion, not more
A thicker nail also fits better and shortens the effective working length

opciones.etiqueta: Nail · Number and position of the locking bolts
criterios: Static at both ends: it controls length and rotation, which the nail does not guarantee on its own
Bolts further from the fracture lengthen the working length and make it more flexible
Dynamising allows axial compression with load, but it demands cortical contact

opciones.etiqueta: External fixator · Mechanics of the frame
criterios: Pin diameter: also to the fourth power. Going from 5 to 6 mm changes more than adding a pin
More pins, further apart from each other and closer to the fracture: stiffer
Bar close to the bone: stiffer. Bar further away: more elastic
A second plane or a second bar: stiffer

derivados.titulo: What the classification from Step 2 says

reglas.texto: Complete articular: the articular block demands ABSOLUTE stability. If the metaphyseal component is comminuted, that component demands RELATIVE. Two zones and two principles in one construct.
Partial articular: the involved articular portion demands ABSOLUTE stability — compression or buttress. The rest is solved according to its morphology.
Simple diaphyseal: a reconstructable line. It can go to compression (ABSOLUTE) or to bridging with enough working length (RELATIVE). What does not work is stopping halfway.
Wedge or multifragmentary diaphyseal: a comminuted component. It does NOT allow absolute stability. Bridge it with RELATIVE stability.
Extra-articular: the surface is intact. The decision is played out in the metaphysis: a simple one allows compression, a comminuted one demands bridging.
Malleolar segment: the fibula and the medial malleolus are rebuilt with absolute stability; the syndesmosis is stabilised separately.

Absolute in the articular block and relative in the metaphyseal component. This is NOT a third kind of stability: it is COMBINING BOTH PRINCIPLES IN A SINGLE CONSTRUCT. Lag screws compressing the surface, plus a plate bridging the comminuted metaphysis.
Absolute in both zones: only correct if the metaphyseal component is a simple, reconstructable line. Check that there is no comminution.
Absolute stability throughout the construct: this demands that the whole line be reconstructable and allow compression.
Relative stability throughout the construct: bridging, with the strain spread out and dosed by the construct.

derivados.titulo: The healing biology you are choosing

reglas.texto: Primary or direct healing, with no visible callus. Where the cortices touch, cutting cones cross the fracture following the Haversian systems. In gaps under 0.5–1 mm with strain below 2%, it is filled with woven bone that later remodels.

Secondary or indirect healing, by callus: haematoma and inflammation → soft callus → hard callus → remodelling. Callus is self-stabilising: as it grows it increases the moment of inertia and reduces the strain.
Two biologies at once, each in its own zone: direct at the compressed articular surface, by callus at the bridged metaphysis.
The governing threshold: lamellar bone tolerates only 2% strain.
The governing threshold: soft callus tolerates 10 to 15%; granulation tissue, up to 100%.

derivados.titulo: What this already decides about Steps 4 to 6

reglas.texto: Step 4: anatomical reduction. Step 5: interfragmentary compression. Step 6: an implant that delivers that compression.
Step 4: functional, indirect, atraumatic reduction. Step 5: splinting or bridging. Step 6: intramedullary nail or bridge plate. Step 10: watch for non-union from too much or too little stiffness.

Step 4: anatomical at the surface, functional at the metaphysis. Step 5: compression plus bridging in the same construct. And do not confuse the principle with the implant: one plate can compress in one zone and bridge in another.

Working length increased. It is the dominant lever: omitting the screw next to the fracture on each side leaves the construct almost twice as flexible, in compression and in torsion. In practice, two or three empty holes on each side.
Plate span ratio = length of the plate / length of the fracture. Target: above 2-3 in comminuted fractures and 8-10 in simple lines.
Plate screw density = screws inserted / holes in the plate. Target: below 0.5 in comminuted fractures and 0.3-0.4 in simple lines.
Three screws per main fragment, spread along the fragment. More than three does not raise axial stiffness and more than four does not raise torsional stiffness.
Dynamic locking or far cortical locking: the shaft flexes in the canal and gives motion back to the near cortex, so the callus forms symmetrically at both cortices.
Working length of the nail: with cortical contact it is the distance between the endosteal contact zones; without contact, the whole distance between the innermost bolts.
Pin mechanics: diameter to the fourth power, number of pins, spacing between them, bar-to-bone distance and number of planes. Raising the pin diameter changes more than adding a pin.

Multifragmentary site: the motion is shared between several interfaces and each one carries only a fraction of the strain. This is the scenario bridging was designed for, and it is why the working length works in your favour here.

Simple line: a single interface takes all the motion of the construct. The denominator of the formula is tiny, so either you compress or you lengthen the working length a great deal. There is no middle ground.

esencial.texto: Every internal fixation provides stability, but not every fracture needs the same kind. Stability is not an end in itself: it is a means to a particular healing biology. Choosing between absolute and relative is choosing between two ways for bone to heal.

Strain (ε) = change in gap length ÷ original gap width. The same micromotion produces enormous strain in a narrow gap and small strain in a wide one, or in one spread across many gaps. Each tissue only survives if the local strain stays below its tolerance.

esencial.titulo: The two consequences that look paradoxical
esencial.texto: A narrow gap with motion does not heal: a transverse line with a small separation under bending generates extremely high strain, no lamellar bone tolerates it, and the fracture resorbs. And comminution, paradoxically, helps: the motion is spread across many gaps, the strain in each falls, and callus forms readily.
Do not compress what is comminuted; do not leave what is simple mobile with a narrow gap. The morphology of the line, which you settled in Step 2, dictates which strain strategy is viable.

esencial.titulo: There is no such thing as «mixed stability»
esencial.texto: There are only two kinds of stability: absolute and relative. When an articular fracture also has a complex metaphyseal component, no third principle is invented: ABSOLUTE stability is given to the articular block and RELATIVE to the comminuted component. That is combining both principles in a single construct. Talking about «mixed» as if it were a category of its own leads people to think there is something in between, and there is not.

A complex, multifragmentary or comminuted component does NOT allow absolute stability. There is nothing to compress without devitalising it, and the resulting gaps would carry a strain no tissue tolerates. That component is bridged, always.

filas: The surface must heal without strain; step-off and micromotion generate arthritis.
A reconstructable line: compression closes the gap and gives friction.
It allows no compression: comminution spreads the strain and bridging respects the biology.
It is enough to restore alignment, length and rotation; callus heals it.

esencial.titulo: The levers of the construct, with their numbers
filas: Distance between the innermost screws on either side of the fracture; in a nail, between the endosteal contact zones or between the innermost bolts.
The dominant lever. Omitting the screw next to the fracture on each side leaves the construct almost twice as flexible in compression and in torsion.
Length of the plate / length of the fracture.
Above 2-3 in comminuted fractures; above 8-10 in simple lines.
Screws inserted / holes in the plate.
Below 0.5 in comminuted fractures; below 0.3-0.4 in simple lines.
How many, and how spread, in each main fragment.
Three is enough: beyond that axial stiffness no longer rises, and beyond four neither does torsional.
The locked plate preserves the blood supply and holds weak bone, but suppresses motion at the near cortex.
Elevation of the locked plate off the cortex.
2 to 5 mm reduce stiffness and respect the periosteum; going further increases the lever arm on the screws.
Screws that grip only the far cortex and flex in the canal.
They give motion back to the near cortex and with it a symmetrical callus.
Bending stiffness rises with the fourth power of the radius: it raises stability a great deal, it does not lower it.
Diameter, number, spacing, bar-to-bone distance, planes.
Diameter also rules to the fourth power: 5 to 6 mm changes more than adding a pin.
Titanium has a lower elastic modulus and works somewhat more elastically. Fine tuning, not a substitute for working length.

esencial.titulo: Check it in the AO simulator
esencial.texto: OSapp lets you configure the fracture, the plate and the load, and calculates the gap strain with finite elements. Changing the working length and watching the indicator move teaches this better than any table.

Too stiff — a short plate, screws next to the fracture, a dense construct — suppresses callus and leads to non-union and fatigue failure. Too lax produces excessive strain, resorption and delay. At the right point, micromotion stimulates abundant, rapid callus. Relative stability is designed, not improvised.

esencial.titulo: The implant is a temporary bridge
esencial.texto: No relative-stability construct survives cyclical loading indefinitely. Implant failure is almost never bad luck: it is the sign that the fracture never healed, nearly always through a mechanical error — inadequate stiffness — or a biological one — a devitalised site. The aim is for the bone to heal before the implant runs out.

items: Compressing comminution: it leaves gaps with extremely high strain and suppresses callus. Comminution calls for bridging, not compression.

A short, stiff plate over a simple transverse fracture: it creates a narrow gap with micromotion that heals neither by the direct route — no compression — nor by callus — too stiff. It is mechanical no-man's-land.
Confusing stability with stiffness: stiffer is not more stable in any useful sense; it may be precisely what prevents healing.

esencial.titulo: The gap is the denominator, and it is what gets forgotten
esencial.texto: Strain is motion divided by gap. Almost everyone works on the numerator — how much the construct moves — and forgets the denominator. A multifragmentary site spreads the motion across many interfaces and turns a considerable displacement into small strain at each one; a well-reduced simple line concentrates all the motion in one narrow interface and turns micromotion into enormous strain. That is why a bridged comminuted fracture heals and a nearly reduced, bridged transverse one does not, even with the same implant. And that is why there is no need to ask: the AO type from Step 2 already says it.

esencial.titulo: The trap of the bridged simple line
esencial.texto: It is the commonest construct error and the most expensive. A transverse or short oblique line is reduced almost anatomically, a long plate is applied, and the holes near the fracture are filled. The result is a minimal gap with a minimal working length: the strain at that single interface is extremely high, the fracture resorbs, no callus appears and the plate eventually breaks by fatigue at an empty hole. There are only two coherent answers to this: compress properly, or lengthen the working length a great deal to spread the motion.

esencial.titulo: The asymmetrical callus of the locked plate
esencial.texto: The conventional locked construct does not close the gap uniformly: the far cortex moves and the one under the plate barely does. Callus follows that asymmetry and appears scant and irregular precisely where the implant is. The three described answers are to lengthen the working length, to lift the plate a few millimetres off the bone, and to use dynamic locking or far cortical locking screws, which grip only the far cortex and flex inside the canal to give motion back to the near one.

esencial.titulo: Stiffness and strength pull in opposite directions
esencial.texto: Lengthening the working length makes the construct more flexible, which is what you want, but at the same time it lowers the load the plate withstands before it deforms permanently. And if there is no cortical contact to share load, that flexible construct fails earlier under cyclical loading. Dosing relative stability is always a balance between the two, and it is compensated with a longer plate, with the weight-bearing regimen, or by restoring some contact.

alertas.titulo: A comminuted component does not allow absolute stability
alertas.texto: You classified a multifragmentary fracture and you are choosing compression. There is nothing to compress without devitalising it: you would be left with gaps carrying extremely high strain, callus would be suppressed and the implant would fail by fatigue. That component is bridged.

alertas.titulo: You are compressing a comminuted metaphyseal component
alertas.texto: In an articular fracture with a complex metaphysis, that component allows no absolute stability. What fits is relative: absolute for the articular block, bridging for the metaphysis.

alertas.titulo: Good: you are combining both principles in a single construct
alertas.texto: This is not a third kind of stability. It is absolute in the articular block and relative in the metaphyseal component, each with its own construct: compression above, bridging below.

You classified a simple line. There is no middle ground here: either absolute compression, or a long working length that spreads the motion. The reason is that strain is motion divided by gap, and in a well-reduced simple line the denominator is tiny: a short, stiff plate leaves micromotion that heals by neither route.

You chose relative stability but you have not yet defined how you dose it. The working length, the screw density and the span ratio are not construct details: they are the dose. Without deciding them, the amount of motion is left to chance.

alertas.titulo: Relative stability in the articular block
alertas.texto: This is exceptional. The articular surface does not tolerate micromotion. If the block cannot be rebuilt, consider whether the real indication is a primary arthroplasty.

alertas.titulo: A thicker nail gives MORE stability, not less
alertas.texto: Bending stiffness rises with the fourth power of the radius. If you are trying to spread strain, a thick nail works against you.

alertas.titulo: The locked plate can also be too stiff
alertas.texto: Its advantage lies in osteoporotic bone and in the comminuted metaphysis. But it is a rigid internal fixator: without enough working length it suppresses callus.
The right stability is the one that produces the biology you want, not the one that holds hardest. Stiffer may be precisely what prevents healing.

alertas.titulo: A long working length over a site with no bony contact
alertas.texto: Lengthening the working length makes the construct more flexible, which is what you want, but it also lowers the load the plate withstands before it deforms. Over a multifragmentary site there is no cortical contact to share load, so the implant fails earlier by fatigue. Compensate with a longer plate or by restricting weight bearing.

alertas.titulo: The locked plate produces an asymmetrical callus
alertas.texto: The conventional locked construct closes the gap asymmetrically: almost all the motion happens at the far cortex and almost none under the plate. Callus follows that asymmetry and appears scant and irregular at the near cortex. It is corrected with dynamic locking or far cortical locking screws, by lifting the plate off the bone, or by lengthening the working length.

alertas.titulo: Filling every hole is not safer
alertas.texto: You have planned the working length but not the screw density. With three per fragment axial stiffness no longer rises, and with four neither does torsional. The extra ones only add stiffness, spend bone and remove options for any future revision.

alertas.titulo: A simple line with relative stability: the classic trap
alertas.texto: Step 2 says the line is simple, and here you have asked for relative stability. A single narrow interface takes all the motion of the construct, and callus does not tolerate that strain: the fracture resorbs and the plate eventually breaks by fatigue. Either you compress properly, or you lengthen the working length a great deal to spread that motion over a long stretch.

alertas.titulo: A simple line bridged and with no working length
alertas.texto: This is exactly the construct that heals by neither route: it does not compress enough for direct healing and it strains too much to heal by callus. If you are keeping relative stability, the working length stops being optional.

alertas.titulo: No cortical column to share the load
alertas.texto: A Winquist III or IV means there is no cortical contact left: the implant carries the whole load and the working length is the entire distance between the bolts. Static locking is mandatory, and the weight-bearing regimen has to be defined, not assumed.

reglasCoherencia.titulo: Consistency — articular fracture with relative stability throughout
reglasCoherencia.mensaje: A complete articular fracture with relative stability throughout the construct. The surface does not tolerate micromotion. If the metaphyseal component is comminuted, mark TWO ZONES: absolute for the articular block and relative for the metaphysis.

reglasCoherencia.titulo: Consistency — a complex articular fracture treated as a single zone
reglasCoherencia.mensaje: You classified a complete articular fracture. If there is a complex metaphyseal component, that is two zones with different demands: check whether it really is solved with a single strategy.

evidencia.afirmacion: Conceptual basis: Perren's strain theory, which explains why some fractures heal with callus and others without it, and underpins the distinction between absolute and relative stability.
The superiority of the locked plate over the conventional one is concentrated in osteoporotic bone and the comminuted metaphysis; there is no universal advantage in good-quality bone.

The working length is the factor that most determines the axial and torsional stiffness of a locked plate; omitting the screw next to the fracture on each side leaves the construct almost twice as flexible. More than three screws per fragment does not increase axial stiffness, and more than four does not increase torsional stiffness.

As an empirical guide, the plate span ratio should exceed 2-3 in comminuted fractures and 8-10 in simple lines, and the screw density should stay below 0.5 in comminuted fractures and 0.3-0.4 in simple lines.
Conventional locked plating produces asymmetrical gap closure and, with it, an asymmetrical and inconsistent callus that decreases from the far cortex towards the near one.

Far cortical locking screws induce symmetrical interfragmentary motion through cantilever bending of the shaft, and in an animal model were associated with greater callus volume and mineral content than conventional locked plating.

autoevaluacion.pregunta: Why does a comminuted fracture heal better with relative stability than with compression?
opciones: Because compression damages the periosteum directly
Because the motion is spread across many gaps and the strain at each one falls below the tolerance of callus
Because compression implants are weaker
Because comminution makes it impossible to place screws
autoevaluacion.explicacion: Compressing would create high-strain gaps that do not heal. Spreading the motion across many gaps lowers the local strain and allows callus.

autoevaluacion.pregunta: Which mechanical error turns a plate into «no-man's-land»?
opciones: Using too long a plate
Putting the plate on the tension side
A short, stiff plate over a simple transverse fracture
Leaving too many holes empty
autoevaluacion.explicacion: It leaves a narrow gap with micromotion: no compression for the direct route, and no flexibility for callus. The answer is to compress, or to lengthen the working length.

autoevaluacion.pregunta: Tibial plateau with a depressed articular surface and a comminuted metaphysis. What do you do?
opciones: Mixed stability, which is a third principle for these cases
Absolute for the articular block and relative for the metaphysis: both principles combined in a single construct
Relative throughout, because there is comminution
Absolute throughout, because there is an articular surface
autoevaluacion.explicacion: Only two kinds of stability exist. What is combined are the principles within one construct, each in its own zone. Calling it «mixed» suggests an intermediate principle that does not exist.

autoevaluacion.pregunta: Why does a comminuted metaphyseal component not allow absolute stability?
opciones: Because screws do not hold in the metaphysis
Because there is nothing to compress without devitalising it, and the gaps would be left with a strain no tissue tolerates
Because the metaphysis always heals by callus
Because the locked plate prevents it
autoevaluacion.explicacion: Compressing comminution leaves gaps with extremely high strain, suppresses callus and ends in fatigue failure of the implant. That component is bridged.

autoevaluacion.pregunta: What strain does lamellar bone tolerate?
opciones: Up to 100%
Around 2%
It tolerates none
autoevaluacion.explicacion: That is why direct healing demands almost zero strain: anatomical reduction and compression. Soft callus tolerates 10 to 15%, and granulation tissue up to 100%.

autoevaluacion.pregunta: What does doubling the diameter of an intramedullary nail do to its bending stiffness?
opciones: Doubles it
Quadruples it
Multiplies it by sixteen
Does not change it
autoevaluacion.explicacion: Bending stiffness rises with the fourth power of the radius. That is why reaming, by allowing a thicker nail, increases stability so much.

autoevaluacion.pregunta: What does it mean that callus is self-stabilising?
opciones: That it forms without an implant
That as it grows it increases the moment of inertia and progressively reduces the strain
That it resorbs if the fracture moves
That it definitively replaces lamellar bone
autoevaluacion.explicacion: Each stage creates a lower-strain environment that allows the next. It is a system that stabilises itself, provided there is enough blood supply.

autoevaluacion.pregunta: A relative-stability implant fails by fatigue at four months. What does that mean?
opciones: That the implant was faulty
That the patient bore weight too early
That the fracture never healed, through a mechanical or a biological error
That a stiffer implant was needed
autoevaluacion.explicacion: No construct survives cyclical loading indefinitely. Implant failure is the sign that the bone did not heal in time: inadequate stiffness or a devitalised site.

autoevaluacion.pregunta: Tibial plateau with a depressed articular surface and a comminuted metaphysis. Which stability?
opciones: Absolute throughout the construct
Relative throughout the construct
Two zones: absolute at the surface, relative at the metaphysis
It depends only on bone quality
autoevaluacion.explicacion: It is the classic two-zone pattern, along with the pilon and the complex distal humerus. Recognising the two zones prevents applying a single philosophy to the whole bone.

autoevaluacion.pregunta: Which of these manoeuvres REDUCES the stiffness of the construct?
opciones: Grouping the screws next to the fracture
Leaving holes empty on both sides of the fracture
Using a shorter plate
Reaming and using a thicker nail
autoevaluacion.explicacion: It lengthens the working length and spreads the strain. The other three increase stiffness, which is the opposite of what relative stability is after.

autoevaluacion.pregunta: Which is the lever that most determines the stiffness of a bridge plate?
opciones: The material of the plate
The working length: the distance between the innermost screws on either side of the fracture
The total number of screws
The thickness of the plate
autoevaluacion.explicacion: Omitting the screw next to the fracture on each side leaves the construct almost twice as flexible, in compression and in torsion. No other lever changes so much for so little.

autoevaluacion.pregunta: A screw density below 0.5 in a comminuted fracture — what does that mean exactly?
opciones: That smaller-diameter screws are used
That fewer than half the holes in the plate are filled
That the two ends are left free
That locked and conventional screws are alternated
autoevaluacion.explicacion: It is screws inserted divided by holes available. Filling them all gives no more stability: it gives more stiffness, less callus and no margin for revision.

autoevaluacion.pregunta: How many screws per main fragment actually contribute stiffness?
opciones: One
Two
Three: beyond that axial stiffness no longer rises, and beyond four neither does torsional
As many as will fit
autoevaluacion.explicacion: The fourth and fifth screws buy no stability: they spend bone and holes. What does matter is spreading them along the fragment instead of grouping them next to the fracture.

autoevaluacion.pregunta: A transverse line reduced almost anatomically and bridged with a long plate — why does it not heal?
opciones: Because the plate is too long
Because the gap is minimal: with one narrow interface, any micromotion gives extremely high strain
Because graft is missing
Because titanium is too elastic
autoevaluacion.explicacion: Strain is motion divided by gap, and there the denominator is tiny. Either you compress properly, or you lengthen the working length a great deal to spread that motion.

autoevaluacion.pregunta: Why does the conventional locked plate produce an asymmetrical callus?
opciones: Because titanium behaves differently at each cortex
Because the gap closes mainly at the far cortex and barely under the plate
Because locking screws are stiffer
Because it is always placed on the tension side
autoevaluacion.explicacion: Callus follows that asymmetry and appears scant exactly where the implant is. It is corrected by lengthening the working length, lifting the plate a few millimetres, or using dynamic locking or far cortical locking screws.

autoevaluacion.pregunta: Lengthening the working length makes the construct more flexible. What does that cost?
opciones: Nothing
It lowers the load the plate withstands before it deforms, and without cortical contact it fails earlier by fatigue
It increases infection
It always prevents early weight bearing
autoevaluacion.explicacion: Stiffness and strength pull in opposite directions. It is compensated with a longer plate, with the weight-bearing regimen, or by restoring some bony contact.
